item.title: The Silent Crisis of Human Reproduction
item.lead: The demographic layer of the dossier posits that digital substitutes not only shift time and money but can also alter expectations regarding relationships and family.

blocks.text: The dossier describes physical relationships as high-threshold: they require time, involve uncertainty, allow for rejection, and entail emotional vulnerability. Digital environments, in contrast, offer immediacy, predictable interfaces, and a defined transaction. According to the source, this asymmetry can become appealing to individuals who struggle with the risks of physical contact.

The hypothesis that follows is economic in nature: when a synthetic alternative appears cheaper, faster, or safer, it can reduce the demand for the original, more challenging alternative. The dossier applies this substitution model to romantic partnerships. It suggests that a portion of the energy that would otherwise be invested in dating, relationship formation, and family planning may shift towards digital consumption.

The source refers to patterns such as social withdrawal, hikikomori-like isolation, and low birth or marriage rates. These references in the dossier are primarily illustrative; the provided text does not offer a detailed statistical analysis that directly attributes such phenomena to adult-tech. For scientific use, a separate research design would be necessary here.

Philosophically, this section revolves around a choice between two conceptions of human connection. In one conception, connection is a fragile, slow, and non-tradable good. In the other conception, proximity is facilitated by technology and rewarded via market mechanisms. The dossier explicitly selects the first interpretation as a normative benchmark.
